title: MB7-18271
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is appealing the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his refugee protection claim.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), is appealing the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his refugee protection claim.
He is presenting what he claims to be new evidence in support of his appeal.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) sets aside the RPD determination and substitutes the determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, namely that XXXX XXXX XXXX is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA.

In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the appellant alleges that he fears the authorities in his country by reason of his membership in the UDPS political party and his photography work for human rights organizations.

The appellant alleges that he was arrested by police officers of the Agence nationale de renseignements (ANR) [national intelligence agency] on May 26, 2016, while he was participating in and taking photographs of a protest organized to denounce President Kabila's government.
The appellant alleges that he was put in prison, beaten and abused until XXXX XXXX, 2016, when an ANR inspector from the same tribe as his helped secure his release for a certain sum of money.
The appellant left his country on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and came to Canada, where he claimed refugee protection.
The RPD rejected his refugee protection claim on the grounds that the appellant's allegations were not credible.
Before the RAD, the appellant submits that the RPD erred in its assessment of his credibility, for reasons that will be detailed later in the Analysis section, if necessary.
Alternatively, the appellant also submits that the RPD erred in failing to assess the sur place aspect of the refugee protection claim.

For these reasons, the appellant is asking the RAD to set aside the RPD determination and grant him refugee protection or to refer the matter to the RPD to be heard by a differently constituted panel.
On January 22, 2018, the RAD issued a decision in this case, confirming the RPD determination and dismissing the appeal.

The appellant applied to the Federal Court for judicial review of the RAD decision, and, with the consent of the parties, the Court referred the matter to the RAD for a hearing before a differently constituted panel, on the basis that "... the RAD erred in law in its analysis of the applicant's sur place claim." (File No. IMM-715-18)

The role of the RAD is to review RPD decisions on a correctness standard after conducting its own analysis of the record in order to determine whether the RPD erred, as the appellant alleges. The exception to this rule occurs in situations where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in making findings that require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral testimony it hears. In these situations, the RAD must show a measure of deference to the RPD findings (Canada v. Huruglica, F.C.A., A-470-14). If I find that the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage, I will explain how in my analysis. NEW EVIDENCE The appellant submitted to the RAD documents that he argues are new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, which states as follows: "On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection."
paragraphs.heading_before: STANDARD OF REVIEW AND RAD'S ROLE

paragraphs.text: In addition to the explicit conditions set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the RAD must also consider the implicit conditions regarding the admissibility of new evidence as established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Singh (M.C.I. v. Parminder Singh, 2016 FCA 96), and in particular, in this case, the criteria of credibility and relevance of new evidence.

The first document is a Response to Information Request COD505818.FE, dated July 10, 2017, from the IRB Research Directorate, titled Situation of people returning to the country after they either spent time abroad, claimed refugee status, or were seeking asylum (2015-July 2017).

This document is subsequent to the RPD decision. I accept it as evidence before the RAD since, in any case, it is part of the most recent National Documentation Package on the DRC, dated July 31, 2018, which I will take into account in my analysis.

Following the Federal Court decision in this case, the appellant sent the following documents to the RAD: A. Certificate bearing testimony, signed by the Secretary General of the UDPS political party on November 13, 2018. This document attests to the appellant's involvement in the party in the DRC, and repeats the information already contained in Exhibit C-1 submitted to the RPD (see page 95 of the RPD record). I do not accept this document as evidence because it repeats the evidence already filed on the record and is therefore irrelevant. In addition, the appellant does not explain why it was not available at the time of the hearing before the RPD or, if it was, why it was not submitted. B. Certificate of membership from the UDPS Party of Canada, certifying that the appellant is a member of the party in Canada, dated October 19, 2018. C. Attestation from the president of UDPS Toronto, dated November 30, 2018, indicating that the appellant is an active member of the Party in Canada. D. UDPS Ontario membership card issued in the appellant's name. E. Eight receipts for UDPS Canada membership fee payments, issued to the appellant, dated from January to July 2018. F. Ten photographs showing the appellant with members of UDPS Canada, taken at a party meeting in Ontario on October 20, 2018.

I accept documents B to F as evidence. In my opinion, these documents are new in the sense that they demonstrate the appellant's ongoing involvement in the UDPS in Canada since the RPD's decision and are relevant to my decision in this refugee protection claim.
Given my decision, it will not be necessary for me to assess whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the credibility of the events that the appellant allegedly experienced in the DRC.
I am of the opinion that the determinative issue in this case is whether the appellant is a sur place refugee.
In my opinion, after analyzing all the evidence presented, the answer to this question is yes, for the following reasons.
In its decision, the RPD failed to analyze the sur place aspect of this case, for which the appellant criticizes the RPD in paragraph 29 of his memorandum.

The first RAD panel did so at paragraphs 35 and 36 of its decision and rejected the refugee protection claim on this ground. The Federal Court subsequently ruled that the RAD had erred in this regard, but did not elaborate on its reasons.

The RPD, in paragraph 9 of its reasons, does not attach probative value to the certificate of membership in the UDPS in Canada (Exhibit C-4, page 98 of the RPD record) in order to demonstrate the appellant's involvement in that party while he was in the DRC. However, it does not rule on the credibility of the appellant's involvement in the party in Canada.
In my view, there is no reason to doubt the appellant's active involvement in the UDPS in Canada.

To begin, Exhibit C-4 demonstrates this, and the new evidence before me, exhibits B to F, further demonstrates this point. I have no reason to doubt the authenticity and content of these documents, issued in Canada.

Furthermore, the document in Tab 14.3 of the National Documentation Package (which the appellant wishes to submit as a new document) indicates that a secret document from the DRC Ministry of the Interior instructs security chiefs to arrest government opponents, including members of the UDPS, and suggests torture be used "with discretion."
The same document indicates that persons who are sent back to the DRC are questioned by the ANR upon arrival, in particular concerning what they were doing abroad and the reasons for their return.

It is obviously difficult to determine in this case what the DRC authorities know about the appellant's political activities in Canada, or to determine what they might learn by questioning the appellant if he were sent back to the DRC.

However, I find that the evidence presented is sufficient to conclude that there is a serious possibility, that is to say more than a mere possibility, that the DRC authorities may know or learn that the appellant has been actively involved in the UDPS in Canada for almost two and a half years now. And that he therefore may be subjected to the abuse mentioned in the documentary evidence as a result of said political activities.

I also find that the evidence shows that, in the appellant's case, the Congolese state protection would not be adequate, since the appellant fears the Congolese government and its representatives, more particularly, ANR agents. The documentary evidence (see Tab 2.1 of the IRB's National Documentation Package on the DRC) indicates widespread corruption and impunity among security forces in the DRC.

Finally, I do not believe that an internal flight alternative would be available to the appellant in the DRC. I have already determined that the documentary evidence mentioned above demonstrates that the appellant would be questioned by security officials upon arrival in the DRC and that a serious possibility of persecution could immediately follow. There would therefore be no place in the DRC where the appellant could even go, let alone settle, without there being a serious possibility of persecution, if he were to return to his country.

In light of the foregoing, I conclude that the RPD's decision is erroneous, and that the appellant has demonstrated that he has a well-founded fear of persecution by reason of his political opinion if he were to return to the DRC.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the RPD determination and substitutes the determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, namely that XXXX XXXX XXXX is a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA.

The appeal is allowed. Normand Leduc Normand Leduc December 20, 2018 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 RAD.25.02 (April 9, 2013) Disponible en français RAD File No. / N° de dossier de la SAR: MB7-18271 4
